title: Effects of carbohydrate ingestion and carbohydrate mouth rinse compared with placebo on physiological, psychological and neuromuscular parameters during high-intensity interval training – a randomized controlled crossover trial
summary: Carbohydrates are an important energy source during exercise. There is also evidence that simply rinsing the mouth with a carbohydrate solution can influence how hard exercise feels, presumably via the brain and without the carbohydrates being ingested. In this study we compare how a carbohydrate drink, a carbohydrate mouth rinse and a placebo during intense interval training affect perceived exertion, running performance, blood glucose, lactate, heart rate and jump performance. Endurance-trained adults run on a track at four visits. At the first visit their personal running speed is determined. At the three further visits they run the same interval session at this speed, once with a drink, once with a mouth rinse and once with a placebo. The order is determined by chance. Finally, a 400 m run with maximal effort follows.
conditions: No diseases are investigated. The study is conducted in healthy, endurance-trained adults. It examines acute physiological, metabolic, neuromuscular and subjective responses to high-intensity interval training depending on carbohydrate ingestion and carbohydrate mouth rinse.

interventions.name: Carbohydrate drink. Participants complete a high-intensity interval training session on a running track (4 x 3 x 400 m, 1 minute rest between intervals, 3 minutes between series) at an individually determined target pace that is to be held constant. In the breaks between interval series they drink,

Carbohydrate mouth rinse. Identical interval session as in group 1. In the breaks between interval series participants rinse their mouth with 25 ml of a 10% maltodextrin solution without swallowing it.

Placebo. Identical interval session as in group 1. In the breaks between interval series participants receive, per series, 100 ml of water containing 0.2 g citric acid and 0.2 g sodium chloride without carbohydrate.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Previous experience in endurance training
Voluntary participation and written informed consent
Full legal capacity and understanding of the nature, scope, significance and consequences of the study
Exclusion criteria:
Acute injuries or severe diseases that affect quality of life or physical performance capacity, in particular cardiovascular, pulmonary, renal or metabolic dysfunction, neurological or psychiatric disorders, advanced degenerative diseases of the musculoskeletal system, and incompletely healed sports injuries
